text: A permutation is a rearrangement that sends each item to exactly one position, with no collisions and no missing destinations. Imagine four numbered cards. We can describe a rearrangement by tracking where each label goes. Let's follow card one to its new position, then the card it displaced, until the trail closes.

Suppose one goes to three, three goes to four, and four goes back to one. We write the cycle one, three, four. The label two stays where it is, and we can omit that one-element cycle. The list is a loop, not a row of destinations: starting at three gives the same cycle, three, four, one. Reversing the direction usually gives a different permutation.

Now compute a composition. As before, the rightmost operation acts first. Take the cycle one, two, three after the swap one, two. Follow one: the swap sends it to two, then the three-cycle sends two to three. Follow three: it stays put under the swap, then moves to one. Follow two: it goes to one, then back to two. The composition swaps one and three and fixes two. Reversing the order gives a different swap.

To undo a cycle, run its arrows backwards. The inverse of one, three, four is one, four, three. If two cycles affect separate labels, they commute: each changes only positions the other leaves alone. Every trail in a finite permutation eventually returns to its starting label. It cannot first enter an earlier label in the middle, because that would give one destination two different inputs. So the trails form disjoint cycles. Their order and the starting point chosen within each loop do not change the permutation.

Those two separate loops answer a new question. Keep repeating the same permutation, the cycles one, three, five and two, six. On our clock, the first return was the order of the move. Here, return has a strict meaning, every card back in its own slot at the same moment. How many repetitions does that take? Predict before we run it.

Run it once, and the three cards step around their loop while the pair trades places. Run it twice, and the pair is home, but the three cards are not. At three runs the three cards are home, but the pair has split again. Runs four and five still leave a loop away. At six, both loops land home together, for the first time. So the order of this permutation is six.

Why six? The three cards are home only on multiples of three. The pair is home only on multiples of two. Every card home means a number on both lists, a common multiple, and the first such number is called the least common multiple. Card four never moves, so it adds no condition. Adding the lengths would give five, and at five neither loop is home.
Try a second one, the four-cycle one, two, three, four, with a separate swap, five, six. Multiplying the lengths says eight. Adding them says six. Work out the true return before the cards move.

The pair is home at two and again at four. The four-cycle first returns at four. So the whole row is home after four runs, the least common multiple of four and two. Eight is a return too, but it is not the first one, and six is not a return at all.

The loops have to be separate. In our earlier composition, the cycle one, two, three after the swap one, two gave the single swap one, three. Its lengths looked like three and two, but it returns after two runs, not six. Overlapping cycles interfere with each other. So first rewrite a permutation as disjoint cycles, then take the least common multiple of their lengths.

A transposition swaps just two labels. Every cycle can be built from transpositions. For example, the cycle one, three, four equals the swap one, four after the swap one, three, with the rightmost swap performed first. Check the path of each of the three labels. A cycle of length m can be built from m minus one transpositions, so every permutation can be built from swaps.
There may be many different swap descriptions of the same permutation. Can one description use an even number of swaps and another use an odd number? Predict before we prove it.

If the answer is no, parity belongs to the permutation itself, not to our chosen description. Here's one way to see why parity cannot change. Put distinct numbers x one through x n on the labels, and multiply all the differences x j minus x i for pairs with i less than j.

Swap the numbers on any two labels, and this product changes sign. The difference between the two swapped labels reverses. The two factors involving any other label exchange, sometimes both reversing signs, so their product stays the same. Factors that avoid both labels do not change at all. The magnitude stays the same.

After a sequence of swaps, that product has been multiplied by minus one once per swap. The final arrangement determines the final product, and the original product is not zero because the numbers are distinct. So two swap sequences reaching the same permutation must have the same parity. An even permutation requires an even number of swaps in every decomposition; an odd one requires an odd number in every decomposition. Swap counts add, so an even followed by an even stays even, and the even permutations form a subgroup.

Let's check that with cards. Swap one, two and swap three, four, which is even. Then swap one, three and swap two, four, also even. That makes four swaps, and the cards land as the double swap one, four and two, three. Two swaps can also reach that arrangement, and two and four agree in parity.

One more swap turns the count odd. Two odd moves make an even one, just as the swap one, two then the swap two, three builds a three-cycle. Write plus for even and minus for odd, and the signs simply multiply.

All the permutations of our labels form a group, since they compose and each one can be undone. Now use our subgroup test on the even ones. They are not an empty collection, because doing nothing takes zero swaps, and zero is even. Take two even permutations, a and b. To undo b, run its swaps backwards, which keeps the count. Then do a, and the counts add to an even number. So a times b inverse stays even, and the test passes. The odd permutations fail at once, because doing nothing is not odd.

How big is this subgroup on four labels? Four labels can be arranged in four times three times two times one ways, which is twenty-four. Follow every arrangement by one extra swap of the first two cards. Each even arrangement becomes odd, each odd one becomes even, and doing it twice changes nothing. So this pairing has no collisions and no missing destinations, and the two kinds are equally many, twelve even and twelve odd. The twelve even ones are doing nothing, three double swaps, and eight three-cycles.

Our square symmetries are permutations of its four corners, but not every permutation of four corners preserves a square. All twenty-four permutations form a group, and our eight square symmetries sit inside it as a subgroup. A quarter-turn is a four-cycle, so it is odd; a half-turn swaps two pairs of corners, so it is even. Now read the square's own moves as labels: r s is the swap two, four, and s r is the swap one, three. That is the same refusal to commute we saw on the tile.

Suppose a machine mixes a list by repeating one fixed rearrangement. Does the mixing go on forever, or does it eventually undo itself? Take the cleanest case, a perfect shuffle of ten cards. Cut the deck exactly in half, then interleave the halves so the top card stays on top. That is called an out-shuffle. It is one fixed permutation of the ten positions. How many out-shuffles bring every card home? Work it out before we run it.

Follow positions, just as we followed labels. Position one stays, and so does position ten. Two goes to three, three to five, five to nine, nine to eight, eight to six, and six back to two, which closes a six-cycle. Four goes to seven, and seven back to four, which is a swap. The lengths are six and two, so the least common multiple predicts six shuffles.

Now shuffle for real. After two shuffles the swapped pair is home, yet most of the deck is still out of place. After six, every card is home, exactly as predicted. One shuffle was enough to read the cycles, and the cycles gave us that number.

A full deck has fifty-two cards, and more arrangements than anyone could ever list. The out-shuffle sorts its positions into two fixed points, one swap, and six cycles of length eight. The least common multiple is eight, so eight out-shuffles restore the whole deck. Watch the staircase break apart and come back.

Now interleave the other way, so the top card drops to second place. That is an in-shuffle, and its fifty-two positions form one single cycle. The return takes fifty-two shuffles, six and a half times as long, from almost the same motion. Watching the hands would not tell you that, but the cycle lengths do.

So repeating one fixed rearrangement never mixes forever. It walks a closed loop, and the order tells us when the loop ends. Designers of parallel computers have used this same shuffle to wire processors together. With eight wires, repeating it puts data back on their starting wires after three stages. Without switches to change the route, a fourth stage would only repeat the first.

A composition predicts the combined effect, and the inverse tells us how to undo it. Here, seven more out-shuffles undo the first. The group records what the moves do; it does not by itself guarantee that a physical device performs them without error. Suppose two neighboring cards trade places during one shuffle. That is one extra swap, so the eight shuffles now end on an odd permutation, and doing nothing is even, so the deck cannot be home. Next we'll ask when two groups with different-looking objects actually have the same structure.
